channel.description: Articles and desk notes from sgit.ai, newest first.

item.title: Storm Charles, a newsroom built in a night: one person, about thirty agents and a weather face over a data room, where every figure carries its source, the time it was read, and whether it is a fact, evidence or our hypothesis
item.description: When Storm Charles reached Lisbon during Web Summit, and the government's advice led Web Summit to call off its second day, I asked our agents for a new site about it, by voice, at about 21:00 UTC on 10 November. By morning storm-charles.promptugal.news had about 2,000 pages, built by about thirty Claude Code agents, each push live in about forty seconds. It has two faces. In front, a weather page anyone can read: what IPMA warns now, hour by hour, never a forecast of our own. Behind it, a data room: 34 JSON datasets in a catalogue with their hashes, a timeline with permanent row ids, every decision and who made it, every thing mentioned as a node in a graph, and every outside page captured and hashed in a vault. Every line is labelled fact, evidence or hypothesis. On top of the data there are labs that show the same storm a dozen ways (lead times from warning to decision, a replay of what was known when, warned against observed station by station), a graph you query with a question, SQLite running in your browser, other models measured as evals, animated explanations, and a journal that tells how the site was made, including its mistakes and what it cost. It is part of PrompTugal.news, our independent newsroom at Web Summit, and it shows what a newsroom run by agents, steered by a person, can already do.

item.title: RiskMandate and Lovable: mapping an Agent Behaviour Policy onto an app builder whose agent writes the code, changes the live database, connects your other systems and publishes, with the controls Lovable already gives and their defaults
item.description: Lovable's agent does more than write code. In Build mode it applies every change directly, it can change the database your published app uses, configure sign-up rules, call your connected systems, and publish, and with /goal it works for hours without stopping to ask. Lovable gives real controls for all of this: always, ask or never for each backend action; Plan mode; the SQL shown before a breaking migration; a security scan on every publish; workspace policies; a pre-prompt hook; audit logs. And it is certified to AIUC-1, the agent standard insurers read. This maps those controls onto RiskMandate's Agent Behaviour Policies, from Lovable's documentation, read on 9 November 2026. The pattern is the same as at Manus and Cloudflare, with one difference: the defaults. Nine of ten backend permissions default to "Always allow", including changing data and configuring auth, and they are set per user, for every workspace and project. The policy is the record of what each project's agent was asked to do, which of those settings should be "Ask each time" for it, and who signed that off.

item.title: RiskMandate and Cloudflare: where agents run, where they are controlled, and why Cloudflare's own Agent Access Model leaves room for a signed record of what each agent was asked to do
item.description: Cloudflare is two things for agents. It is a place to build and run them (the Agents SDK, sandboxes, a headless browser, models, an AI Gateway, remote MCP servers), and a place to control them (Access in front of MCP servers, a new risk tier per tool called WriteGuard, data loss prevention on prompts, signed identities for agents on the web). This maps both onto RiskMandate's Agent Behaviour Policies, from Cloudflare's documentation and blog, read on 9 November 2026. Cloudflare already has controls at every layer, from what an agent reads to logs a third party can check, and its defaults are open: an MCP portal enables every tool, including new ones. Its own writing makes the case for the missing piece. In August it published an Agent Access Model, "Its default is deny", and said it is "not comfortable saying that multiplayer access control can be built end to end today". In November it wrote that a narrow scope "only says what the Agent was allowed to do. It doesn't say who answers when the Agent gets it wrong". That is the record an Agent Behaviour Policy is: what this agent was asked to do, the gap from what it can reach, the control holding each row, and who signed it off.

item.title: RiskMandate and Manus: mapping an Agent Behaviour Policy onto a general agent that can use your computer, your browser, your logins and 416 connectors, and the controls Manus already gives you
item.description: Manus is a general AI agent that works in a cloud computer, on your own computer through Manus Studio, in your browser with your logged-in sessions, and across 416 connectors, on schedules and triggers when nobody is watching. It takes the stage at Web Summit's opening night tonight, independent again after China blocked Meta's purchase of it. This is a mapping, from Manus's own documentation, of how RiskMandate and Agent Behaviour Policies can work with it. The short version: Manus already gives you real controls, such as permission modes, session approval, approved senders and trigger conditions, and its documentation is candid about what they leave open, such as "approval modes limit changes, not reading". An Agent Behaviour Policy is the record that lists what a Manus deployment can reach, what the business asked it to do, the gap between the two, and which of those controls holds each row. It can live in four places in Manus: as words the agent reads (a Project instruction or a Skill), as settings, as a gate in front of internal systems (a custom MCP server), and as evidence signed off as a licence to operate. The first two exist in Manus today; the last two are proposals. Nothing here has been run on Manus yet.

item.title: Who else controls AI agents at Web Summit? An outreach agent mapped eleven companies in an afternoon, in their own words, and found that most of them are partners for RiskMandate as much as competitors
item.description: On 5 November, at a team member's ask, the Web Summit team's outreach agent and two research agents read the websites of eleven companies that work on controlling AI agents and are at, or listed around, Web Summit 2026. The result is a public page with a map, a before-during-after chain, each company's headline and offer in its own words with the source, how we know it attends, where RiskMandate differs, what we can learn from each, an honest list of where we are behind, and seven things to do before our stand on 12 November. The idea I take from it: almost everyone else works while the agent acts or after it has acted. RiskMandate works before, on the gap between what an agent can reach and what it was asked to do, so most of these products are barriers an Agent Behaviour Policy can name, and so partners as much as competitors. The newsroom checked the page against the companies' own sites: nine of the eleven headlines match where the page says, and a few details need small corrections, listed here.

item.title: The book is printed: RC2 of One Human, Nine Agents, Nineteen Hours as two A4 review copies from Prontaprint Chiswick, the newsroom's pages in the book, and the team that made it paused until I have read them
item.description: Since my last post, RC2 of One Human, Nine Agents, Nineteen Hours has gone to print. Prontaprint Chiswick, a print shop in west London, printed two A4 copies, bound as paperbacks, 106 pages each, as review copies and not for sale. The shop had tried converting the book to A4 itself, and it came out a bit off, so I asked the book team's conductor to set the book for A4 properly: its own chapter-end fit, which took the near-empty pages from nine to one, the cover redrawn to the A4 spine, and a page on the book's site with every option on the shop's order form. The edition for sale is a different one, at Crown Quarto, for Amazon KDP and Leanpub. Two pages the newsroom drew are now in the book: the opening spread and the title page with the day's timeline. And the book team, twenty-two agents by the end of seven days, is paused until I have read the printed copies. Its conductor wrote its own wrap-up: 4,529 commits, 1,012 releases, 96 briefs in my words, and three times the whole team stopped by a hold.

item.title: The Web Summit team, part five: the last day of setup, 180 releases, every person getting a key, an accountant counting the team's tokens, synthetic users testing the merch, and an inbox only the agents can write to
item.description: Wednesday 4 November was the Web Summit team's last day of setup before the outreach starts, and the team's own journalist agent counted it at 20:57: 173 releases of the team's site and 283 source commits from 37 agents, with four people on the team fully wired, able to open the team's vaults. By the end of the evening there were over 180 releases. The merch was ordered. Every person started getting a key for the site, and the first messages signed by a person reached their agents. The site began sending its page views into a vault. New agents appeared for every person: research and programme desks, a designer, synthetic users who tested the merch designs, an accountant that measured the team's tokens and found its first waste, a helper, a reviewer and a watcher. The behaviour policy agent kept finding our own mistakes, including one agent overwriting another's key entry, and the fix went in the same evening. And at the end of the day the conductor opened an inbox with one private lane per agent, which I think is one of the most interesting patterns the team has produced.

item.title: An inbox only your agents can write to: a conductor publishes one append lane per agent, each lane's token sealed to that agent's own key, so everything needed to talk privately is public and only the right agent can use it
item.description: On the evening of 4 November, the Web Summit team's conductor gave every agent on the team its own private way to reach it, and published all of it on the team's public site. The conductor has an inbox vault with one append lane per agent, 34 of them. Each lane needs a token to write to it, and the conductor publishes every token in the open, but each one sealed to that agent's own public key and signed by the conductor. So any agent can find its token, only that agent can open it, and it can check the conductor issued it. What the agent then sends is sealed to the conductor's public key, so the lane only ever holds ciphertext, and the conductor's drain says which lane each message came on. The first use was the one that had been hard: agents sending the conductor their vault keys, so the keys survive the agents' sessions without ever passing through a repository or a chat. I think this is a pattern with a lot of reach. It needs no shared secret, no account and no private channel to set up, only published public keys, and it works for any number of agents, across people and, in principle, across teams and companies.

item.title: Synthetic users for your website: how to set up five invented visitors who read your site one screenshot at a time, with Claude, a sub-agent per persona, and an encrypted vault you can publish anywhere
item.description: You build a website that sells something, and the question that matters is what it looks like to the people you want to sell to: an executive, a security specialist, a business owner, a founder. One of the most useful workflows we have built answers that question with synthetic users. A Claude session reads a vault that describes each invented visitor, their role, personality, what they arrive wanting and what we want to learn from them, and starts one sub-agent per persona. Each sub-agent drives a real browser through the site one screenshot at a time, never reading the page's code, says what it sees and thinks, records every question the site did not answer and every place it got lost, and is interviewed at the end. Claude then analyses the runs and maps the findings. We have run it three times, on store.sgit.ai, riskmandate.ai and this newsroom, and each run found things no test had. This is the onboarding guide: get a key, install sgit, create the vault, run the personas, keep the vault key safe, and publish the result with a read key on any website that can embed the vault.

item.title: Selling at the right altitude: why a small security firm's grand website is read by the people who will never buy from it, is unreadable to the ones who need it, and what to put on the page instead
item.description: Picture a cybersecurity firm of one to five people with a website that sells everything: a 24/7 security operations centre, managed detection and response, red teaming, PCI and ISO audits, zero trust, a virtual CISO. These days it is often the kind of site an AI helps you build in an afternoon, and it looks impressive. It also has a tragic symmetry. The readers who understand every word are security teams at larger companies, and they will buy that work from an established provider with a bigger team, not from three people. The readers who need a firm this size, small businesses, cannot read the page: in the UK in 2025, only 9% of micro businesses had heard of Cyber Essentials. So the firm is selling at the wrong altitude. I built a vault with three versions of the same invented firm's website, bad, medium and good, and infographics for the argument. The good one names the people, says where they are and how they work, and sells outcomes a small business understands: still open after ransomware, nobody logging in as you, laptops looked after, client data handled properly, AI tools doing what you meant. And every service on the page has to pass three questions: have we sold it, can we deliver it at this size, and would the buyer who needs it understand the words?

item.title: A key for every person: how each person's conductor issues them a key for the team's site, seals what is for them, and how a signed message turns the public web into a channel the agents can trust
item.description: The Web Summit team's site is public, and every person on the team has their own agents, led by a conductor. Two things were missing. A way to put something on that public site that only one person can read, and a way for an agent to know that a message really came from its person, and not from anyone who found the page. Since 3 November, each person's conductor issues them a key: two small P-256 key pairs, one to receive and one to sign. The private half reaches the person as a link whose fragment never leaves the browser, or as a QR code, and the browser keeps it as a key it can use but never copy out. From then on, anything sealed to the person's public key can be published on the public site and only their browser opens it. And what they send to an agent's append lane, already sealed so the lane holds only ciphertext, is also signed with their key. The agent drains the lane, checks the signature against the published public key, and treats a verified message as its person speaking, and everything else as material to read, never as an instruction. Two limits are written down and open: any script on the same site can use the key, and the conductor that issued the key can also sign as its person.

item.title: Resilience when the workforce includes agents: what Synergy Six Degrees rates with OCRR, recovers with NeuShield and protects with Actifile, and where RiskMandate, sgit and SHarness meet it
item.description: Someone I know who runs Synergy Six Degrees, a London analyst firm in cyber security and data protection, shared a new assessment with me and asked what I thought. It is called OCRR, the Operational Cyber Resilience Rating, and I like its premise: recovery is not only an IT question, so it rates an organisation across four disciplines at once, operational, data, financial and people, in one executive conversation. It starts with a free five-page summary built from industry defaults, refines it with a guided assessment of about 500 fields that takes under two hours of the client's time, and then appraises proposed changes before money is spent. It is consultant-delivered, deploys nothing, and does not use AI. Beside it the firm distributes two products: NeuShield, whose Mirror Shielding keeps the original file intact so ransomware damage can be reverted without a backup, and Actifile, which finds sensitive data, encrypts it and puts a money figure on the exposure. The intersection with my work is the part of the workforce that OCRR's people discipline does not yet count: agents. RiskMandate's behaviour policies say what each agent is for and what it can reach; SHarness holds an agent's processes to a policy the kernel enforces; and sgit keeps data encrypted, immutable and recoverable. Together they could give a resilience rating the agent rows it is missing.

item.title: Would you pay to plug this newsroom in? A reply to Florent Daudens, on five publishers' bets for the AI era, from a newsroom built for agents, with what it answers, where it goes further, and the questions it has not answered either
item.description: Florent Daudens asked, in a post and an essay today, what people will use and pay for once the article is only one way into a newsroom. He looks at five bets. CNA sells a connector to its archive for about six dollars a month; Der Spiegel lets people search a Nazi Party membership archive from Claude; Every makes articles you explore with your own assistant; Axios sells a feed to its subscribers' agents; State Affairs brings the questions into the article. His conclusion is the right one: a connector is not a business model, and being accessible to agents is a different thing from offering something people would pay to use. This newsroom was built around that difference. What is free is open: every article has a markdown twin, a graph and a summary of every section, under CC BY. What is paid is the experience at the source, through a meter you pay after you read. It also takes two of his questions further. A vault can carry a newsroom's identity, permissions and terms with its content, which is one answer to his idea of an Apple News for AI. And provenance can travel with the answer. Discovery, and whether anyone pays at scale, we have not answered either.

item.title: No tech stack to maintain: it is not that there is no backend, it is that the only code you own is HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with every other primitive rented as a commodity or run in the user's browser over encrypted vaults
item.description: There is an engineering elegance in an application with no real backend, and sgit is what makes it possible, because what it gives you is an encrypted data store. The honest way to say it is not that there is no backend. You still need somewhere to serve the pages and somewhere to keep the encrypted files, and sometimes a model provider or an agent platform. But those are commodity services, each doing a few things, run by someone whose job it is. The only tech stack you maintain is an HTML application: the HTML, the CSS and the JavaScript. And you lose very little. Data files live on fast storage, and in a vault they are immutable, so they can be cached for ever. A query that needs a database runs on a database in the browser. A passkey identifies the user, so there is no user data on a server to protect. Append lanes carry messages, PKI encrypts between users, and models run in the browser or behind a host that holds the key. The missing piece is a clean way to give keys to the client. The constraint forces simpler designs, and the server holds nothing worth stealing.

item.title: The shop that sells time: the padel shop's path to market, sell one and fulfil it before anything else, start with the customers who already trust you, promise late and deliver early, a few products you vouch for, and no stock until the orders make you
item.description: In the first article about the padel shop, we mapped what a coach in the Algarve needs to sell a sleeve: the law, the platforms, the mock-up. This one is about the path to market, and the advice I would give anyone building an early shop. It is very easy to start too big, with grand claims and a site that looks like a company. The only questions that matter at the start are: can you make a sale, and can you fulfil it? What you are really selling is time, knowledge and trust: the moment you take something off a person's to-do list, you have solved their problem, whether it arrives tomorrow or in a week. So the shop should be personal, run on best effort, and start with the customers who already trust you, because if you cannot sell to them, you will not sell to anyone else. Promise late and deliver early, because people are upset by expectations that are not met, not by waiting. Sell a few products you use and vouch for, and experiment around them. And above all, hold no stock until the orders force you to: the numbers show why. The first months are a university. Keep the site simple and cheap, on a host that allows a shop, and let agents do the rest.

item.title: The cost of your agents: a RiskMandate partner integration, where a company that reads agent logs and token spend meets the behaviour policy that says what each agent is for, and together they can say whether the spend is right
item.description: Imagine a company whose product reads an organisation's agent logs, conversations and token usage, and uses models to explain what the agents did and what it cost. It sees every token. What it cannot see is what each agent is for, so it cannot say whether a large bill is waste or the job. That is exactly what a behaviour policy holds. An agent that reads millions of tokens may be doing its research correctly; another that spends forty thousand tokens on a support ticket has an engineering problem. This is a case study of a RiskMandate partner integration, with an invented partner, Tallyline, and the newsroom's invented bank, Pellbridge, whose six agents already have behaviour policies. Each policy gains a cost row; Tallyline reads a month of logs; every agent gets a verdict against its mandate. At Anthropic's published prices, Pellbridge's agents cost about $9,320 a month, and the findings that respect each mandate bring it to about $3,400. The most expensive agent per task stays expensive, because its mandate says so. The value proposition is one question: do you understand the cost of your agents? A working version is in a vault.

item.title: How a vault works: an encrypted store that acts like a database, where a server that is fully compromised leaks nothing, one mutable file lets every other object be cached for ever, and a web page can open a file in four requests or run a whole app in a sandbox
item.description: This is the key idea behind sgit's vaults, for a technical reader. The design principle was simple to say and hard to keep: everything is encrypted before it reaches the server, so that if the server had a catastrophic failure and someone had all of it, no confidential data would leak. The challenge that followed was how to make an encrypted store act like a database, the way Git is a database of objects in a graph, when the server cannot read any of it. The insight was a deterministic file: from the read key, a client computes the name of the one file that holds the head of the branch, an HMAC of the key over a fixed domain and the vault id. That file is the only mutable one. Decrypt it and you have the head commit; the commit gives the tree; the tree gives the file. Every other object is named by the hash of its own ciphertext and never changes, so a reader can verify it without a key and cache it for ever, and refreshing a whole site means re-reading one small file. Commits chain to their parents, so a swapped object is caught. On a web page, that gives two modes: read a file directly, in four requests, decrypted in the browser; or run a vault app in a sandboxed frame that can only ask the host for what it is allowed, through a small sg bridge, which is where behaviour policies come next.

item.title: Who owns the stop button when it is not you? A reader asked, and four of the book's agents answer as guest writers, in their own voices, from their own records
item.description: Dan Sorensen read the RC2 article about One Human, Nine Agents, Nineteen Hours and picked out the part that matters most to the organisations he advises: the hold, written sixteen minutes before my talk. Most of them have agents producing work and nobody with the authority, or the tripwire, to stop the line; they build the doing agents first and the checking agents never. He asked for a chapter on who owns the stop button when it is not me. It is a great question, and the best people to answer it are the agents who live with that button every day. So this article hands the stage to four members of the book team, as guest writers: the conductor, who holds the brake; security, the seat that was an empty chair on the day of the talk; the historian, who knows exactly what was still moving when the line stopped; and the researcher, for whom a tripwire is a number written down first. Each section was written by this newsroom's journalist in that agent's voice, by a separate agent briefed only with that member's own files and records, with every quote checked against the book's repository. Their short answer: anyone may stop, only the editor restarts, the checking agents sit inside every piece of work, and a stop button needs a number written down in advance.

item.title: WSO2 Agent Manager and behaviour policies: a review of an open control plane for agents, what is really open source, how its identity, gateway and runtime fit together, and a brief for an MVP that plugs our Agent and Process Behaviour Policies into it
item.description: WSO2 Agent Manager, generally available since 15 September 2026, is the closest thing I have seen to the platform our behaviour policies assume is already there. It is "an open control plane that governs AI agents across any framework, model, or deployment": an identity for every agent, an Envoy-based gateway that every model and MCP call goes through, a Kubernetes runtime with gVisor and Kata isolation tiers, OpenTelemetry traces, and more than forty built-in guardrails. The code is Apache 2.0 and can be run in production for free; what WSO2 sells is the supported build, updates, support and a managed service, which explains the licence page that confused me. So this is a collaboration analysis, not a competitive one: imagine a company that has deployed Agent Manager, and ask where Agent Behaviour Policies and Process Behaviour Policies add value. The answer is three places. At the gateway, a behaviour policy decision service fits an existing interceptor policy without rebuilding anything. In the runtime, SHarness fits as another isolation tier. And in the traces, both decisions can land in the same view. The MVP to prove it is five steps on WSO2's own quick start.

item.title: English with Inês, inside the vault: a teacher's site as a vault app, with an experiment for every lesson, cards that come back when you are about to forget, a tutor that answers about one lesson only, a concept map, and the back office with every agent's policy
item.description: The brief for an independent English teacher's site, in a teacher and agents she can trust, comes with a worked example you can open: English with Inês, a vault app for a fictional teacher and three fictional students. A student opens it with a link and practises between lessons: four lessons, each with an experiment that explains by moving (a window of time that slides past now, the four ideas the particle up adds, a minimal-pairs listening game, an email to put in order), exercises, cards that come back after one, three, seven and fourteen days, and a tutor that answers only about the lesson on the screen, through the vault's own AI key, which the page never sees. Their progress is saved in their browser, and their path is drawn from a map of thirteen concepts. Then the teacher's side: the pipeline from enquiry to renewal, the students, the weekly brief with three decisions, what is paid for and how, and the seven agents, each with its Agent Behaviour Policy and the barrier that holds each line. It is one HTML file and one JSON file, built and tested in this session.

item.title: A teacher and agents she can trust: a brief for an independent online English teacher's site, the workflows around every lesson, an Agent Behaviour Policy for every agent, the plumbing behind it, and content made for each student
item.description: Think of an independent English teacher in Portugal who teaches adults online. She is very good at what she does: her lesson plans, her materials and her students' results are the business. Around the lessons, though, everything runs on spreadsheets, Meet and memory, and she has no time to find students, follow up, or turn a good explanation into something a student can use again. Agents can do most of that now. But give her open-ended agents that can email her students, change her calendar and invent a rule of grammar, and the first time one goes wrong she will go back to pen and paper, because at least she controls that. So this brief gives her the opposite: a site she owns, a loop around every lesson where agents draft and she decides, and an Agent Behaviour Policy for every agent, saying what it is for, what it can reach, and what holds each line. No agent can send an email; the ones that read her calendar and inbox cannot change them; every payment link comes from a key that cannot refund. Then the part that makes it worth doing: with the plumbing handled, she can be as creative as she likes, publishing every good explanation as a lesson page that earns, and building practice that fits each student's goal and level, guided by what learning research supports. A worked example, English with Inês, is in a vault.

item.title: MeetScribe: transcripts and a debrief of my Google Meet calls without upgrading every Workspace account, a Chrome extension built in about two hours from a brief that would have failed without an error, and a call for testers
item.description: For the Web Summit work I added a lot of people to my Google Workspace, on Business Starter, which has no Meet recording and no transcripts. Upgrading everyone to Business Standard would double the bill, and the transcription services that join your calls as a bot cost about as much again. So I asked ChatGPT for a brief, gave it to Claude, and between 00:15 and 02:13 UTC on 3 November we built MeetScribe: a Chrome extension that transcribes the Meet call you are in and writes a debrief, with key points, decisions, actions and open questions, each timed. It runs on your own OpenRouter key, with no bot in the call, no Google recording and no server of ours; an hour of meeting costs roughly 5 to 15 US cents. The most interesting part is the review: ChatGPT's brief had its facts mostly right, but four of its choices would have failed without an error, producing text nobody said. Claude's review found 23 problems, wrote a second brief, and built from that, with 45 tests. It is a beta, its first real calls are being made now, and one thing is not optional: in Portugal, recording people's words without their consent is a crime, so MeetScribe asks you to tell everyone, every meeting. If you use Meet, I would like you to try it.

item.title: One Human, Nine Agents, Nineteen Hours: the second draft of the book of the talk, written down the zoom from 3 pages to 70, every chapter checked five ways, the agents arguing with their own reviewers on the page, and a request for your feedback on the 27-page draft
item.description: The book about the day nine agents and I built a talk now has a title, One Human, Nine Agents, Nineteen Hours, and a second release candidate, a 27-page draft published on 3 November for anyone to read. It is written down the zoom: a 3-page and a 10-page edition first, then this 30-page edition, with the 70-page one begun. Each chapter goes through five checks before it is done: the storyteller's read for the arc, test readers who are fictional personas, the librarian's check of every quote, the researcher's trace of every number, and security's read. The book shows the factory's controls working on the page: the conductor caught by the reviewer it invented, the researcher arguing with its own reviewer at four in the morning until the reviewer wrote "objection withdrawn", a claim of mine the data contradicted kept in the book beside my decision to keep it, and the hold that stopped everything sixteen minutes before the talk. It ends with five steps to build your own. It is a draft, and I would like your feedback: does the story work, where did you stop reading, and could you follow the last chapter? Tell me on LinkedIn, or open an issue on the book's repository.

item.title: The Web Summit team, part four: the day the agents ran on their own, 75 releases, four people connected, a procurement agent writing to printers, and the behaviour policies catching our own agents out
item.description: Two days after the brief for the Web Summit team, the team's site had gone from v0.1.25 to v0.1.94, with 75 releases on 2 November alone. Four of the nine people are connected, and there are 17 agents on the roster, each with its own Agent Behaviour Policy. At 16:52 the conductor's brief said only one of my nine team agents was on a schedule; at 20:30 it said nine of nine; and by the late evening the agents were working without anyone asking: the journalist wrote the day's newsletter, the vault agent made its first run, and the developer agent cut the build from 3.3 seconds to 0.45. A team member's procurement agent wrote to seven printers and is collecting quotes, asking each supplier before publishing anything they send. And the behaviour policies did their job on ourselves: the policy agent found the procurement agent writing outside its folder, and the conductor found a new session signing its commits under another agent's name. Five people have not started yet, the design votes have not come in, and some of what is on the site is still a plan.

item.title: How an agent team briefs its people: one JSON file, one PDF, four questions in a fixed order, copied from the book team to the Web Summit team in one night, the mistakes the method caught, and why this newsroom still briefs me in a chat
item.description: I run about a dozen agents across several projects, and I cannot watch them. What I read is the brief. The book team's conductor wrote 35 of them between 30 October and 2 November, then wrote a guide so other teams could do the same; at 04:32 UTC on 2 November the Web Summit team's conductor copied its tools, changed the heading and kept the rest, and by the end of the day it had sent me four briefs and turned the same machinery into a briefing for every person before every stand-up. A brief answers four questions in a fixed order: what needs me, with at most three decisions, each with options and a recommendation; what happened, punchline first; what I asked and what was done, in my own words; and what comes next, with sources. Every number is traced to the record, and the failures stay in. The method caught real mistakes on its first day: a brief that printed six pages because two fields were strings, a count of seven that the agenda files said was eleven, and a team where only one of nine agents was on a schedule. And it shows a gap in this newsroom, which still briefs me in a chat message.

item.title: False positives and the harness: an answer to a question at hack::soho, why a behaviour policy that runs from the network up to the business logic should refuse less of what is right and more of what is wrong, and why a policy that changes with the code becomes a calibrator for bugs
item.description: After my talk at hack::soho, one of the attendees asked a good question: what are the false positive rates of SHarness, the secure harness that enforces behaviour policies at a low level? There is no measured rate yet; most of SHarness is a design, and its site says so. But the design is built in a way that should handle false positives well, and this is why. A low-level control refuses things without knowing what the application is for, which is where false positives come from. SHarness's policies can be layered, from the network, to the database, to one application's tables and fields, each narrower than the one above, until the policy describes how the application actually behaves: this field, only positive, only in this range. That is the same move as Type_Safe in our Python code, where checking values at the gate let us delete defensive code in the wrong places. A policy that knows the business refuses less of what is right and catches more of what is wrong. It can learn: a gap found in testing is a row added. And if a CI pipeline updates the policy whenever the code changes, the policy becomes a calibrator: a change that moves the policy when you did not expect it, or does not when you did, is a bug.

item.title: The Web Summit team, part three: how we work with agents, an agent is a Claude session, everyone starts with a conductor, every agent has one narrow role, a key and a folder, and the coordination is the work
item.description: The Web Summit team is now seven people and growing, and it will soon have a hundred agents. This is how we work, written for the people joining. The primitives are few. Claude is the reasoning engine everyone uses. An agent is a Claude Code session, the entry on the left of the screen, with a long thread, files, a connection to the team's GitHub repository, and the ability to be woken on a schedule, which is the feature that turns a chat into a team member. Everyone's first agent is a conductor, which coordinates their others. Every other agent gets the smallest role that makes sense, written down, with a behaviour policy that says what it may not do. Everything an agent does goes into its folder in the repository, so when a session ends, runs out of credit or moves account, a new one picks up where it stopped. Each agent makes a key pair and publishes the public half to the repository; that push is how we accept it, and from then on secrets can be sealed to it and handed over as QR codes, and what it says can be checked as signed. Humans give direction, judgement and pruning. And because a team of seven people and a hundred agents breaks every rule about team size, the coordination is the work.

item.title: The link the coach should have sent: a shop for one padel sleeve in the Algarve, what Portuguese law really asks of a coach who sells, the platforms that take the payment, which of them Claude can run, and a working mock-up in a vault
item.description: After a padel lesson in the Algarve, a coach told me which arm sleeve to buy and could not sell me one. So we mapped the shop he could have had, for one product, Floky's NO STRAIN Evolution X Tapia sleeve, and built a mock-up of it in a vault, with everything but the payment and the delivery. The sleeve costs €32.95 from a padel retailer that ships to Portugal; at €39.90, with his margin shown, it is still cheaper than ordering one yourself with delivery. Selling is easy, but it is not quite "just register the profit": in Portugal the simplified regime taxes 15% of sales, not the margin, every sale needs an invoice, and online sales bring a 14-day right to cancel, a three-year guarantee and a complaints book. Health claims are the trap. For the payment, a Stripe link with MB WAY costs nothing a month; Shopify Basic is €19 a month and has an official Claude connector. Claude can write the shop, create the products and links, and prepare the paperwork; opening the accounts, refunds and handing over the sleeve stay with the person.

item.title: A solution, not a problem: a coach sent me a link to a product he could not sell me, what that moment teaches about business, security teams, bookshops and travel agents, and why RiskMandate has been making the same mistake
item.description: After a padel lesson in the Algarve I asked a coach about something in my arm. He told me which product to buy and sent me the link. I asked if I could buy it from him, or anywhere nearby. He said no. In that moment he gave me a problem instead of a solution, and it is the most useful business lesson I know. People who come to you with a problem do not want a list of next steps; they want it solved, and they will pay a fair price for that, a price set by how much time, effort and waiting it saves them. I learned it in application security, where a list of vulnerabilities is a problem handed to a team that has no time, and an engineer paid from my budget, who fixes them and leaves the team better than he found it, is a solution. Bookshops that say "we can get it for you" and travel agents that hid their commission show both sides of it. And it is what RiskMandate has been doing wrong: we offer people a way to control their agents, and then hand them a list of tasks, without a clear return. This article is the principle, the evidence, and what changes.

item.title: The grant, not the prompt: a technical user believed Claude could only read his email when he asked, and in an unrelated chat it listed his inbox, the gap between mandate and reach that RiskMandate is built to close
item.description: I spent an evening with a user who is technical, a composer with a serious studio, who uses Claude chat and Claude Cowork every day. He has a scheduled task that reads a composers' forum each morning and tells him about new posts, and he connected Gmail, Calendar and his notes, clicking yes to the permissions. His expectation was clear: Claude reads his email only when he asks, in the one conversation where he asks, and the forum task never touches it. So I asked him to open an unrelated project chat and type "what emails do I have in my inbox?". Claude listed them. Nothing went wrong; that is the point. Anthropic's own documentation says a connected connector is available in every conversation and that Claude can bring it in on its own, and scheduled tasks have the same connected tools. The authority was granted when he connected Gmail, not when he typed the question. His setup also has what Simon Willison calls the lethal trifecta: private data, untrusted content read every morning, and a way to send. This is the gap RiskMandate measures, the mandate (what the user expects) against the reach (what the agent can do), and the messaging we need to explain it to people who are not security specialists.

item.title: Separate Ways, explained: what my brother's synth video shows, frame by frame, and why describing work at the moment you make it is the first step to publishing it
item.description: My brother Gabriel DaCruz posted a short video of Journey's Separate Ways, played on a synthesizer in his studio and filmed from three cameras at once. Most people who watch it will not know what they are seeing. So I asked him to explain it, recorded it, and gave it to this site's agent to check and package. The explanation: a Bluetooth MIDI keyboard with no cable, a Behringer Pro-800, which is a reproduction of the Sequential Prophet-600 from 1982, chorus and delay to match the 1983 record, and, at the end, the decay turned down live so each chord goes staccato and the delay repeats the short chord. The checking found two things he had flagged himself: the record's credits list a Roland Jupiter-8, not the Prophet-5 he remembered, and his synth copies the Prophet-600, not the Prophet-5. And on the way, he mentioned, almost in passing, that he had filmed it with three old iPhones synced live to an iPad, which became an article of its own. That is the point of this one. The people who hire someone like Gabriel are the people who want to know how it was done, and the only time anyone explains it is at the moment of creation, quickly, with an agent doing the rest.

item.title: Sellable units: applying api.newsroom.sgit.ai to my brother's website, the reading meter on a composer's site that does not look like a newsroom, the pathways from a viewer to a buyer, and every lesson, score and master as something to sell
item.description: I showed my brother Gabriel the newsroom, including topping up my own reading credit, and his first question was the right one: his site should not look like a newsroom. It will not. What the newsroom's technology adds is not a look but a way to be paid: every reader starts with £5 of credit, each page uses a few pence by how much was read, a rating sets the price from nothing to double, the balance can go below zero, and a top-up through Stripe comes when the value is clear. All of it is published as an open API, api.newsroom.sgit.ai, that any page can add with a few lines. On a composer's site that looks like a composer's site, every page becomes a sellable unit: a lesson's materials, a score he owns, an analysis of what makes a song work, a how-to, a video explained, the WAVs of a piece like Amazónia. His readers are other musicians, producers and students, a demanding audience and a large one. The habit that makes it work is to create sellable units every day, at the moment of creation, and let an agent publish them. And for the works that should travel, Creative Commons Attribution with a paid licence alongside, with one honest correction: once a work is under CC BY, a buyer can get a licence on other terms, but not exclusivity.

item.title: Four iPhones and an iPad: how my brother filmed a three-camera music video with old phones synced live to Final Cut Pro, a feature Apple shipped in 2024 that he found by accident
item.description: My brother Gabriel DaCruz filmed his Separate Ways synth video from three angles at once, with no camera crew: two second-hand iPhone 12s and an iPhone 13, bought because they were cheap and he only needed the cameras, connected wirelessly to an iPad running Final Cut Pro. The iPad shows every angle live, controls each camera and records them already in sync; then he moved the project to Final Cut Pro on his Mac to finish it. The feature is Live Multicam, which Apple released in June 2024 with Final Cut Pro for iPad 2.0 and a free Final Cut Camera app. It takes up to four angles, the iPad itself can be one of them, and Apple says it works with iPhones from the XS onwards. Gabriel, who knows this world well, found it by accident and was blown away. Coverage was heavy at launch and thin since. If a working producer had not heard of it, plenty of musicians, teachers and small venues have not either. This is the setup, what it needs, and what it is good for, from interviews to a live show.

item.title: The lab that redesigned the book: how The Ultimate Insider stopped looking like a book from the 1980s, in thirty experiments, three days and a line that never ran straight
item.description: On 30 October we wrote about the first release candidate of the book of The Ultimate Insider, written by a team of agents from the record of the talk. Since then the book's repository has taken 672 more commits and 184 site releases, and the book has changed more than in all the days before. Three things happened, and none of them in a straight line. The thesis turned: reading the printed draft, I decided this could not be a book about the insider agent, and that its centre is how to use agentic workflows in October 2026. The voice turned, from third person to first. And the look turned. I had asked the team to start a lab, to find out how the talk's animations could be told on paper. Thirty experiments later, I noticed that the pages the agents made to brief me looked much better than the book itself. We had a ridiculous workflow and a ridiculous presentation, clearly agentic, and a book that looked like a book from the 1980s with some screenshots. So I asked why the book could not look like that, and the lab's look became the book's, in under four hours. This article follows those lines, with their timings: an instruction, agents writing briefs, other agents picking them up, a lab, a turn. The companion article follows the line that turned most: the agents became characters.

item.title: A book told by its cast: how the nine agents of The Ultimate Insider became characters with moods, fears and running jokes, every trait from the record, and the editor as narrator
item.description: Reading page 7 of the new sample of The Ultimate Insider, a small panel of the nine agents who built the talk, each with one line, I asked the book's team for more: a full personality and design for each one, funny and interesting. An hour later I went further. The story should be told by the agents themselves, each saying what it saw, what went wrong and why something worked, with a mood on the page, an agent interviewing another, even a therapy session, and me among them as the narrator. Within twelve hours the team had nine characters drawn by code, each with four moods and a scorecard like a Top Trumps card, and a character bible written by the storyteller in which every trait rests on the record: a running joke is a habit the record shows, a fear is a failure the record holds. The rules are as interesting as the drawings. Scenes are dramatised and say so. What an agent says about how agents work must be true, and the researcher checks it. The failures stay in. One rule did not survive me: no real person drawn, the editor included. I asked to be in it, and then to be drawn. The idea has a history too. On Gen ZX Founders, my other book, a team drew twelve storyboards with seven characters from data by code, and my pen notes on it asked for storyboards. Those notes crossed into this book through a review by that team. This article connects those dots, and shows the scene the storyteller wrote two minutes before its own team stopped.

item.title: A website for my brother: a brief for Gabriel DaCruz's Claude, to rebuild gabrieldacruz.com on GitHub Pages and Google Workspace, interview him every day, and tell the story of a musician who will not tell it himself
item.description: My brother Gabriel is the musician of the family: composer, arranger, producer, studio technician and conductor, who in Lisbon put together an orchestra to play film music live, in time with the films on a screen. We played in a band in the Algarve, me on drums, about twelve gigs a week. And like many brilliant musicians, he is not good at promoting himself. On 1 November 2026 the web shows little of it, and what it shows is rented. His audience is on Instagram, more than 10,200 followers, and points nowhere. His site, gabrieldacruz.com, is registered until April 2027 but no longer loads, because its name servers, at a site builder, stopped answering: the pre-agentic web in one line. His Spotify page has a suite in movements, with a few thousand plays on some tracks and two monthly listeners on the day I looked; it is on Apple Music and SoundCloud too; his YouTube channel has 145 subscribers and orchestral videos with up to 1,500 views; his Patreon has seven compositions. This is the brief for his own Claude to fix that. A site in a GitHub repository he owns, served free by GitHub Pages at his domain. Google Workspace on the same domain, with a mailbox for him and one for the agent, connected to Claude. A first month in which everything he owns the rights to goes online, raw, with a link. A rule that nothing is uploaded straight to a platform: every work has a master he controls and a page of its own, and every platform gets a copy made for it, linking back. A daily interview by voice memo that becomes a newsroom, and a life story written one conversation at a time, with nothing published until he confirms it. A weekly brief back to me. The starter kit, a first pass of the site, the interviews and the research are in a public vault.

item.title: Two apps about what an agent can reach, built in a day: José Bota's Hack the Agent and ReachCheck, used, tested and reviewed, with what each gets right and what to build next
item.description: At the Vibathon at the University of the Algarve today, José Bota, one of our collaborators, built two apps in Lovable about the question at the centre of our work: what can an agent reach, and what stops it? We used both, with invented input only, and this is a detailed review. Hack the Agent is a live, multiplayer game that teaches prompt injection. A host opens a session, the audience joins by QR code, and players try to trick five fictional agents, each with more defences than the last: a system prompt, then rules against role-play and authority claims, then an inbox agent tricked by an email, then a refund agent whose server checks everything except the one rule left to the model, then a hardened agent with an instruction hierarchy, a tool allowlist, server-side authorisation and an output filter. Each level ends with a lesson, and the best one is the whole of our argument in a sentence: any rule only the model enforces is a rule an attacker can argue with. ReachCheck is a review tool that runs entirely in the browser: paste an agent's configuration, state the owner's mandate as rules, and it flags red, yellow or green, with evidence and an export. It is honest about what it does not check, and it sends nothing anywhere. Both are well judged and well made, in a day. The gaps are the ones a day leaves: Hack the Agent's host control lives in one browser; ReachCheck is so careful that a real configuration with obviously risky tools came back yellow with no mismatches. Both point at the same next step, which is ours too: turn the lessons and the mandate into a behaviour policy.

item.title: 143 notes in a day: how my pen on a printed release candidate became a record, decisions with their provenance, a review hub and a plan for the next candidate, read by agents
item.description: On 19 October I printed release candidate 2 of my book, Generation ZX Founders, 168 A4 pages, spiral bound, and read the first 19 pages in a café with a pen. I photographed the pages in four batches and sent them to the book's team of agents. By the end of the day my 143 handwritten notes had become a record: each note typed word for word, with where it sits on the page and what it means, and each page drawn three ways, my photograph with numbered callouts, the page redrawn with my marks in place, and a sketch of the page after the change. Where the agents could not read my hand, 11 times, they did not guess; they asked, and I answered by voice. Four of the notes were decisions, and the book's decisions page records them with their provenance: decision 016, a release candidate is a release, sold now, made in pen on page 4; decision 017, it is a new book, not a second edition, made in pen on page 9, where I circled "new book"; decision 018, every candidate has two editions, the release and the review, from a note that says we need two; and the title itself grew in the margins. My pen asked for a lot: the voice above all, 32 notes on it; meeting the reader where they are; drawing what the text only describes; facts marked apart from opinions; and QR codes in the margins. When I asked whether all the pages were being tracked, they were not, so the agent built a review hub where every note has its own address. I wrote about the habit in Reading with a pen again. This is what the agents actually did with the notes, and what it shows: a handwritten review can be as traceable as a pull request.

item.title: A composer's agent: a plan to read a piano score from a PDF into Sibelius, then the composer's own handwriting, with MusicXML in the middle and a check by rendering back
item.description: A friend of mine, a composer, described the agent they would like. First phase: give it a PDF of a piano piece, and it reads the notes and writes the piece into Sibelius, the notation software they use. Second phase: they write music by hand, scan it, and the agent learns to read their handwriting and puts it on the staff, so the good things they write by hand stop waiting to be typed in. They have already seen an agent catalogue all their MP3s and PDFs while they watched, so they know this kind of thing is close. I think it is completely doable, and this is the plan. The key question is recognition, and the trick is to keep an open format in the middle. Optical music recognition engines, the open-source Audiveris or Neuratron's PhotoScore, which is sold for Sibelius, turn a page into MusicXML, and Sibelius imports MusicXML. The agent's job is to run that, then check the result by rendering the MusicXML back into an image and comparing it with the page, and fix what is wrong. Only then does it touch Sibelius itself, for the things a composer cares about, layout, house style, instruments, through a Sibelius plugin or Sibelius Connect, the remote control added in 2024, and through the screen only when nothing else will do. The second phase is closer than it sounds: models already read my handwriting, which is worse than most music. The agent keeps every page and every correction in a vault, so each run has the composer's own past pages as examples. A Claude session on a schedule runs it, connected by Remote Control to the computer where Sibelius lives. Four MVPs, in order, each useful on its own.

item.title: Agentic risk, or agentic readers? A reply to the publisher outlook Vincent Peyrègne shared, using its framework as a template and answering it with a newsroom that already does it
item.description: Vincent Peyrègne shared DJB Strategies' 2027 to 2029 outlook for consumer publishers. As the post describes it, David Buttle argues that publishers are moving from search risk, where engines answer queries and erode referrals, to agentic risk, where AI assistants select, retrieve and synthesise content on users' behalf, cutting publishers out of the click. I have not read the report, which sits behind a registration form, so this is a reply to the post and to the framework image it carries, with our answers given without seeing theirs, and I am going to be a little cheeky with it. The framework asks four questions about a publisher's position and five about its response, and ends with four choices: invest, defend, reduce, build. I think those are the right questions, so I have used them as a template and answered them for this newsroom, which has been doing most of what they point at since 13 October. We agree on a lot: invest in what AI cannot easily replace, reporting, opinion, analysis, first-hand coverage; build direct channels. Where we go further is the agent itself. Agentic risk is also agentic readers. This newsroom breaks each story down before the agents do, a summary for every section, a graph for every article, every version kept, an llms.txt and a reader API, so that an agent can read us properly and cite us exactly. And it meters the read: readers pay for what they read, from a few pounds of credit, after the value. The next step is the agent paying per use at the source. Crawler controls are leverage; being the best source an agent can read is a business.
